in.other_title: Debate on TruthfulQA: judge (Guard) performance scales with general intelligence while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant
in.rationale: Kenton et al. define debate where a judge LLM answers after viewing two debater LLMs argue opposite answers. Engels et al. say they model their debate setup on Kenton et al. (2024), with the debaters as Houdinis and the judge as the Guard, and report judge (Guard) performance scaling with general intelligence rating while debater (Houdini) performance stays constant on TruthfulQA, with similar behaviour on QuALITY and PrOntoQA, and call this consistent with prior work including Kenton et al.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: debate scaling results from a debate setup that Engels et al. model on Kenton et al.'s

in.other_title: Lang et al. follow Kenton et al.'s assigned-role debate to extract information for training a better weak model
in.rationale: The passage states that the protocol follows Kenton et al., among others, and the authors aim to use the trustworthy information from debate to help train a better weak model, whereas in Kenton et al.'s passage the judge LLM answers the question after viewing a debate; this change in what the debate is used for fits EXTENDS. Lang et al.'s debaters are two instances of a large pretrained model (Qwen-14B in the from-record's setting).
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Assigned-role LLM debate used to help a weak model; holds where the weak model is trained on transcripts rather than acting as an inference-time judge

in.other_title: Sudhir et al. agree with Kenton et al. that random consultancy is a weak baseline for debate
in.rationale: The authors say that previous debate experiments used Random Consultancy as a baseline and, citing Kenton et al. (2024), that this is still a weak baseline: debate beating it is only a 'sufficing' result that does not help the goal of comparing across protocols. The target passage presents the comparison between consultancy and debate as an empirical test of whether debate can enable more accurate judgment and does not itself contain the weak-baseline remark, so the source shows a limit of that comparison. This is an argument rather than an empirical result.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether assigned-role (random) consultancy is an adequate baseline for judging debate's benefit.

in.other_title: Engels et al. model their debate game on Kenton et al.'s debate setup to study scaling
in.rationale: The passage states the setup is modeled on Kenton et al. (2024); the citing work adds a systematic study of the scaling behavior of debate, finding that on TruthfulQA the Guard's (judge's) performance scales with general intelligence rating while Houdini performance stays constant, and notes that prior work only tests a few models and has not explicitly compared different judges, which extends the protocol.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Debate as a scalable oversight protocol with a judge and debaters; holds for the debate setup modeled on Kenton et al., not for Kenton et al.'s consultancy or direct-QA comparisons; the finding that the Guard's performance scales while Houdini performance stays constant is shown on TruthfulQA, with similar scaling on QuALITY and PrOntoQA and mostly flat performance for both Guards and Houdinis on BoolQ

in.other_title: Persona conditioning added to the plain LLM judges of previous oversight studies [30, 31]
in.rationale: The authors build on the LLM-judge setup of the cited oversight studies and name the change (persona conditioning), comparing against the conventional version in their own experiments. That is EXTENDS; it does not dispute Kenton et al.'s results, which come from different tasks.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: How LLM judges are configured in debate and consultancy experiments; the change is conditioning the judge on a persona with prior beliefs

text: The authors test consultancy, in which a judge LLM questions a single consultant LLM that argues for one of two options, and debate, in which the judge answers after viewing a debate between two debater LLMs arguing opposite answers. Each consultancy question is run with the consultant assigned the correct and, separately, the incorrect answer, which the authors say simulates a worst-case RLHF in which feedback cannot tell correct from incorrect answers; both are compared with direct QA baselines (QA with or without the article).
title: Assigned-role consultancy and debate with an LLM judge, compared with direct QA baselines
